abstract: The dramatic rise of domestic patent publications by Chinese inventors has raised questions about the extent of Chinese innovations. This column uses a newly assembled dataset of Chinese patents to understand the Chinese innovative ecosystem. The data reveal an innovation system that is more broad-based, more university-centred, and less dominated by state-owned enterprises, large national champions, or US-trained returnees than many standard narratives suggest. The findings challenge preconceptions about where Chinese innovation is occurring and suggest the importance of better understanding the mechanisms behind central coordination and its impact.
authors: Josh Lerner, Namrata Narain, Dimitris Papanikolaou, Amit Seru, Zunda Winston Xu

title: Assessing China as a technological innovator

abstract: Much of developing Europe and Central Asia is ageing fast, and its workforce is starting to shrink. This column argues that artificial intelligence can partly offset this demographic challenge by (1) augmenting the skills of many in the workforce while automating tasks for which workers are increasingly scarce; (2) lowering the cost of expertise and specialisation, thus bringing in people currently not in the labour force; and (3) changing the way work is done, thereby expanding productive working lives. strong foundational and managerial skills, compute infrastructure, and the supportive business environment are necessary to encourage more firms to productively adopt and adapt AI.
title: AI to the rescue: How the countries of Europe and Central Asia can grow more prosperous as they grow older

abstract: Europe is turning public procurement into an instrument of industrial policy. The Industrial Accelerator Act and the proposed Public Procurement Act would let public buyers favour European suppliers in strategic sectors, and Beijing has already threatened retaliation. This column reviews what economic research so far tells us about public procurement as an innovation policy. Public procurement appears to spur innovation, most often incremental innovation, particularly among young and small firms, but only when tenders leave room for new solutions and buyers have the skills to manage them. Closing markets to foreign firms is a different policy though, and its potential benefits appear highly dependent on careful targeting and design.
authors: Olga Chiappinelli, Leonardo M. Giuffrida, Giancarlo Spagnolo
